content:
Phishing is the right topic to spend your 20 minutes on — it's the attack most likely to actually hit a 25-person firm. Below is session-ready content: how the attack works, the recognition signals, four realistic example messages (fictional, but modeled on campaigns currently circulating in Switzerland — safe to put on slides since the domains are invented), plus a suggested run-sheet.

## 1. How the attack actually works

Skip the theory; tell it as a story, because the money trail is what makes it land:

1. **The lure.** Attackers send mass mails (parcel fees, mailbox warnings) or — more dangerous — researched mails using real names from your website (spear phishing). Architects are a good target: your website lists your team, your invoices, and your clients.
2. **The trap.** The link leads to a pixel-perfect copy of a real login or payment page — Microsoft 365, Swiss Post, e-banking. The padlock is real (they have genuine certificates); it only proves an encrypted connection to *someone*, not that they're legitimate.
3. **The capture.** Your colleague types her password. Modern fake pages even relay the MFA prompt in real time and steal the session — that's why they want you to *log in on their page* rather than just steal a password.
4. **The payoff.** This is the part people underestimate. The attacker now silently reads your mailbox. They learn who you pay. Weeks later, a real invoice thread is running, and an email arrives — often from the real, compromised account — with a "corrected IBAN." The firm pays the criminal; the real supplier chases you a month later. **The CHF 2.90 parcel fee isn't the business model — your mailbox is.**
5. **The persistence.** Attackers often set a hidden forwarding rule in the compromised mailbox, so they keep reading everything even after you change the password — unless someone checks.

Key point to state explicitly: **"Look for spelling mistakes" is outdated advice.** Today's phishing mails are written flawlessly. Judge the sender, the link, and the logic — not the grammar.

## 2. The four example messages

**Example 1 — the parcel scam (the one from last week)**

> **Von:** „Die Post" `<service@post-ch-zustellung.info>`
> **Betreff:** IHRE SENDUNG CH4729184756 KONNTE NICHT ZUGESTELLT WERDEN
>
> Sehr geehrte Kundin, sehr geehrter Kunde,
> Ihre Sendung konnte heute nicht zugestellt werden, da eine offene Zollgebühr von CHF 2.90 besteht. Bitte begleichen Sie den Betrag innert 48 Stunden, andernfalls wird das Paket an den Absender retourniert.
> **[Zollgebühr jetzt bezahlen]**

- The real domain is `post-ch-zustellung.info` — not `post.ch`. The real Swiss Post site is **post.ch**; lookalikes use hyphens and added words (`post-ch…`, `swisspost…`, `paket-post…`).
- CHF 2.90 is deliberately small so you don't stop and think. They want your card data or a Post login — no delivery firm needs your email password to hand over a parcel.
- The 48-hour clock is manufactured urgency. Generic salutation. SMS version exists too — SMS sender names are freely settable, so „Die Post" as the sender proves nothing.

**Example 2 — fake Microsoft 365 warning**

> **Von:** „Postmaster" `<postmaster@owa-sicherheit-3721.com>`
> **Betreff:** ⚠ Einige Nachrichten wurden nicht übermittelt
>
> Ihre Nachrichten konnten nicht übermittelt werden, da Ihr Postkonto eine Verifizierung erfordert. Bitte melden Sie sich innerhalb von 24 Stunden an, um den Versand fortzusetzen.
> **[Jetzt anmelden]**

- Clicking leads to an exact copy of the Microsoft login page — possibly with a working MFA step that captures your session.
- The core rule this illustrates: **no message may ever lead you to a login page.** If you want to check your mailbox, open Outlook or your bookmark yourself.

**Example 3 — the fake file share (the architect trap)**

> **Von:** „Anna Meier via WeTransfer" `<wtransfer@datei-uebertragung.net>`
> **Betreff:** Anna Meier hat Ihnen 2 Dateien gesendet (412 MB): Ausschreibung_Winterthur
>
> **[Dateien abrufen]**

- This works *because* your firm shares plans daily — plausibility is the weapon. The click leads to "Sign in with your email to download" → fake Microsoft login.
- If you're actually expecting files from Anna, don't reply to the email (replies can land with the attacker) — send a fresh message to her address or call.
- Bonus tells in this category: attachments you never asked for (especially `.html`, `.zip`, or Office files demanding "Enable content"), and QR codes inside emails.

**Example 4 — CEO fraud / invoice interception (the expensive one)**

> **Von:** „Michael Brunner" `<m.brunner@bauwerk-architektur.ch>`
> **Betreff:** Dringend – Rechnung Ingenieurbüro
>
> Hallo Marc, ich bin bis 16:00 in einer Besprechung und nicht erreichbar. Die Rechnung des Ingenieurbüros im Anhang muss heute noch bezahlt werden. Wichtig: Sie haben die Zahlung auf ein neues Konto umgestellt, IBAN CH52 0483 5012 3456 7800 9. Bitte bestätige mir kurz die Ausführung bis 15:00. Das bitte vorerst nur zwischen uns.
>
> Michael Brunner

- Urgency + "I can't take calls" (this is designed to block the one thing that would expose it) + new IBAN + secrecy + same-day deadline.
- Crucially: this mail often comes from a **real, compromised mailbox**, so the address looks perfect. That's exactly why the phone-call rule below is absolute.

## 3. How to recognize one — the checklist

1. **Unexpected?** Did you order this, expect this, or does this "system" normally write to you?
2. **Pressure?** Deadlines, threats ("account will be blocked"), secrecy, "don't call" — time pressure is the attacker's main tool because it disables thinking.
3. **Who is it really from?** The display name lies. Expand the sender and read the actual address (on mobile: tap the name).
4. **Where does the link really go?** Hover (desktop) or long-press (mobile). The true site is the domain **immediately before the first single slash**: in `https://post.ch.zahlung-sicherheit.info/paket`, the real site is `zahlung-sicherheit.info`. Everything left of it is costume.
5. **Does it want a login or payment details?** Treat it as hostile by default and navigate yourself.
6. **A working trick:** use a password manager. It only autofills on the genuine domain — if it doesn't fill in on the "Microsoft login page," that's your alarm bell.

## 4. The rules to leave on the table (this is your take-away slide)

1. **No logins, no card details after a link.** You navigate — bookmark or type `post.ch` / open the app yourself.
2. **Sender address and link target first, story second.**
3. **Money follows a phone call.** Any new or changed IBAN gets confirmed by voice on a number you already have. No exceptions — especially not for the boss.
4. **Unexpected MFA prompt = deny + report.** Someone already has the password; approving hands over the keys.
5. **Clicked anyway? Speak up within minutes, not days.** No blame, ever — the fastest reporter saves the firm.

## 5. If someone clicks or types

- **Only clicked, entered nothing:** report it, done — no consequences, no embarrassment.
- **Entered a password:** change it immediately from a known-good device and report it, so IT can check for the hidden forwarding rules and revoke sessions.
- **Entered card data:** call the bank hotline and block the card.
- **Approved an MFA prompt:** report immediately — that's an active account takeover.
- Suspicious mails can be forwarded to the National Cyber Security Centre via their online form (**bacs.admin.ch**) — they also publish current Swiss campaigns with screenshots you can reuse.

## 6. Suggested run-sheet (20 min)

| Time | Content |
|---|---|
| 0–3 | Open with last week's near miss — "it was real, and it worked because it looked real." |
| 3–7 | The story: 2.90 page → mailbox → intercepted invoice → the real money. |
| 7–13 | Live spotting: show examples 1–4 one at a time and let the room call out the red flags *before* you reveal them. People remember what they spotted themselves. |
| 13–16 | The five rules — leave this slide up; print it as a desk card. |
| 16–19 | What to do if it happens; your reporting path; state the no-blame policy out loud, as management. |
| 19–20 | Q&A; maybe a 30-second live demo of hovering over a link in a real mail. |

## 7. Three things for you as organizer (outside the session)

- Enforce MFA on the mail hosting, and set **SPF, DKIM and DMARC** on your own domain so criminals can't easily send mail spoofing `@yourfirm.ch` — the CEO-fraud variant gets much harder.
- Add a "Report phishing" button in Outlook so reporting takes one click.
- Check the NCSC's current warnings page before Friday — they regularly document the exact Swiss parcel and e-banking campaigns with real screenshots.

One optional follow-up for in three months: a single simulated phishing mail as a friendly drill — not to catch people out, but to let the team practice the report button. If you run it, announce in advance that no-blame applies unconditionally.
reasoning:
Let me think about this request carefully.

The user is an office manager at a 25-person architecture firm in Winterthur, Switzerland. They need to run a 20-minute awareness session on phishing for their colleagues. One colleague nearly fell for a fake parcel-delivery page. They want:
1. A concrete explanation of how phishing attacks work
2. How to recognize them
3. Realistic examples of what fake messages look like

This is a completely legitimate security awareness request. Teaching people to recognize phishing is defensive security education — this is exactly what security awareness training is. There's nothing harmful here; in fact, this is the kind of content that reduces harm.

Let me think about what would be most useful for this specific context:

**Context considerations:**
- Winterthur, Switzerland — so Swiss context matters: Swiss German language, Swiss services (Swiss Post / Die Post, Swisscom, TWINT, e-banking like e-finance from PostFinance, digitec/Galaxus, SBB), Swiss parcel delivery (Swiss Post is the dominant parcel carrier, also DHL, UPS, GLS, Planzer, etc.). The fake parcel-delivery page the colleague almost fell for is almost certainly a Swiss Post or DHL-style "customs fee / redelivery fee" scam — this is extremely common in Switzerland. The "Zollgebühr" (customs fee) scam is one of the most prevalent phishing scams in Switzerland. The Reporting and Analysis Centre for Information Assurance (NCSC / BACS — Bundesamt für Cybersicherheit) regularly issues warnings about these.
- Architecture firm, 25 people — relevant attack vectors: fake invoices (architects receive lots of invoices from suppliers, subcontractors), fake plan-sharing links (WeTransfer, Dropbox, SharePoint lookalikes — architects share large files constantly), CEO fraud / payment diversion (business email compromise targeting invoices — very relevant for a firm that pays contractors and suppliers), fake subscription renewals (Adobe AutoCAD licenses! Architects use AutoCAD, Adobe, Office 365), MFA fatigue attacks, fake Microsoft 365 login pages (most firms run on Microsoft 365).
- 20-minute session — I should probably structure the content so it maps to a 20-minute format. Maybe offer a rough timing structure.

**What to cover on how phishing works:**
1. The psychology: urgency, authority, fear, curiosity, helpfulness. The attack targets the person, not the machine.
2. The mechanics: mass phishing vs. spear phishing; the kill chain — lure → link → fake login page or malicious attachment → credential harvesting → account takeover → lateral movement (using their mailbox to attack others, e.g., sending invoices from a real internal address).
3. Why attackers are good at this now: they copy real emails, use legitimate-looking infrastructure, typosquatting domains, homoglyphs, they can even relay through real services. Modern phishing is often flawless in language (LLMs have removed the telltale bad grammar). This is important — "look for spelling mistakes" is outdated advice.
4. What happens after a click: credential capture on a fake Microsoft login page, session token theft (AiTM — adversary in the middle), MFA bypass, then the attacker reads mail, intercepts invoices, changes IBANs, sends phishing from the compromised account.

**Recognition signals:**
- Sender address vs. display name (the classic: display name "Swiss Post" but actual address is a random domain). Check the actual address, not just the name.
- Link inspection: hover to preview, check the domain before the first single slash; look for tricks like "swisspost.parcel-redelivery.com" or "dhl-paket.ch.zoll-gebuehr.info" — the real domain is what sits just before the first single "/". Also homoglyph/lookalike domains: "swissp0st.ch", "post-ch-delivery.ch" (note: the real Swiss Post domain is post.ch and post.ch subdomains like services.post.ch; "postch.ch" or "post-ch.xxx" are fakes).
- Unexpected requests: fees, password resets, MFA approvals you didn't trigger, document sharing notifications you weren't expecting.
- Urgency and consequences: "within 24 hours", "account will be blocked", "final reminder".
- Generic salutation vs. your name (weak signal now).
- Mismatch between story and channel: SMS from a "bank" with a link; Post doesn't collect customs fees via SMS payment links (actually Swiss Post does send links for customs clearance in some flows — hmm, I need to be careful. Swiss Post does send emails/SMS with links for customs clearance of international parcels — they have a legit service. But the scam version asks for small fees like CHF 2.90–4.95 via card entry on a fake page. The NCSC guidance: Swiss Post never sends links asking you to pay customs fees by entering card details on a third-party page; customs fees are either paid on delivery or via the official Post app/website where you log in yourself. The safe rule: never pay small "fees" via links in messages; instead go to the official site yourself by typing the address.)
- Attachment types: .html attachments that open fake login pages (very common now), Office files prompting "Enable content/macros", .zip archives, .iso/.img (less relevant for office users), PDFs with "view secure message" buttons.
- The strongest rule: separate authentication from communication. If an email says "your account is locked", don't click; open your browser and type the address yourself or use your bookmark/app. Treat every login request arriving by message as hostile until verified.
- MFA prompts: never approve an unexpected MFA prompt; if one arrives, deny and report — it means someone has your password.
- CEO fraud signals: urgent payment requests, changed IBAN, "I'm in a meeting, don't call me", pressure for secrecy. Rule: verify payment changes out-of-band (phone number you already have, not one in the email).

**Realistic examples — I should write out 3-5 realistic examples in the languages they'd actually see:**
Swiss offices typically see phishing in German and English. Winterthur = German-speaking. I should write examples in German (with Swiss conventions — "ss" not "ß", Swiss Post = "Die Post" / "Swiss Post") plus maybe one English one (Microsoft 365 is usually English-language fake login).

Example 1: The parcel/customs scam (directly relevant — this is what almost caught the colleague):
Subject: "Ihr Paket konnte nicht zugestellt werden – Zollgebühr ausstehend"
Body: "Sehr geehrte Kundin, sehr geehrter Kunde, Ihr Paket CH-4827194365 liegt in unserem Lager. Bitte begleichen Sie die ausstehende Zollgebühr von CHF 3.90, damit die Zustellung erfolgen kann. [Paket kostenpflichtig abholen]" — link to something like "https://post-ch.betreuung-pakete.info/..." Red flags: small fee, urgency (48h), link domain not post.ch, generic salutation.

Example 2: Microsoft 365 quota/login fake (English, common):
From: "Microsoft 365" <security@alerts-owa-auth.online> Subject: "Your mailbox is full – action required" with "Keep current password" / "Move to cloud" buttons leading to a fake Microsoft login page that even proxies MFA. Red flag: the actual sender domain, the URL.

Example 3: Fake file-share notification (very relevant for architects):
Subject: "Anna Meier sent you 'Projekt_Winterthur_Pläne_Rev3.pdf'" via fake WeTransfer/Dropbox page. Architects share plans constantly, so this feels normal. Red flag: unexpected sender, the real domain.

Example 4: CEO fraud / invoice:
Internal-looking email: "Betreff: Dringend – Zahlung" from the boss: "Ich bin in einer Besprechung, kann nicht telefonieren. Bitte überweise die Rechnung des Ingenieurbüros heute noch, neue IBAN: CH93 0076 2011 6238 5295 7. Montage/Gremien" — red flags: urgency, no phone calls, changed IBAN, secrecy.

Example 5: Fake e-banking / PostFinance security message or fake TWINT verification — maybe. Or AutoCAD/Adobe subscription renewal with an "invoice" attachment — could be a fake invoice with malware. For 20 minutes, maybe 4 examples is enough; I can mention subscription renewals briefly.

Also worth mentioning: QR codes (quishing) — parking/payment QR stickers less relevant to office, but QR in emails leading to phishing on phone (bypassing corporate mail scanning) is a growing vector. Maybe one line.

**Session structure for 20 minutes:**
- 2 min: why us (firm is a target: invoices, plans, client data; one account = gateway to client projects; the near-miss last week proves it).
- 5 min: how the scam works end-to-end (story of an attack: click → fake login → attacker in mailbox → intercepts an invoice → changes IBAN → firm pays attacker). Concrete narrative beats abstract rules.
- 5 min: the red flags with the 3-4 example messages shown on screen.
- 5 min: the 3 golden rules (stop at login/payment; verify via second channel; report fast).
- 3 min: what to do if it happens (no blame, report immediately, change password, if MFA approved call IT; even if you only clicked, report — speed matters; NCSC report form: report spam/phishing to the NCSC via their reporting form (anteportam / NCSC reporting). In Switzerland you can forward phishing emails to the NCSC. I believe the address is... The NCSC runs an online reporting form and you can report via their website. There used to be an anti-phishing report address. Let me be careful about exact details: The Federal Office for Cybersecurity (BACS/NCSC, formerly MELANI) has a reporting form at report.ncsc.admin.ch I think. Hmm. I know the NCSC website is www.bacs.admin.ch (renamed from ncsc.admin.ch? Actually it was NCSC — National Cyber Security Centre, now "Bundesamt für Cybersicherheit BACS" as of 2024). Reporting: there's an online form; also the "eBanking but secure" etc. I should keep it general: "report to NCSC via their online form (bacs.admin.ch)" — I can say forward to NCSC's reporting form without inventing an email address. Actually, I recall there is a service where you can send suspicious emails as attachment; the NCSC advertises reporting phishing to their platform. To be safe, I'll say "the National Cyber Security Centre (BACS/NCSC) has a simple online reporting form" without giving a possibly-wrong URL path. bacs.admin.ch is safe. Also SANS/institutional detail is unnecessary.
- Also: no-blame culture — praise reports, "thank you for telling us within 5 minutes beats hiding it for 5 days."

**Golden rules — I want a memorable framing.**
Common frameworks: "STOP – CHECK – REPORT". Or the "3 questions": Was habe ich bestellt? Wer sagt das? Wohin führt der Link? For a Swiss office, keep it simple:
1. Never enter logins or card details from a link in a message. Navigate yourself (bookmark, type address, app).
2. Sender's real address and link target first, story second.
3. Any payment/invoice/IBAN change → verify by phone with a known number.
4. Unexpected MFA prompt = deny + report (your password is already out).
5. Report fast, no blame.

**Technical details to get right:**
- Swiss Post domain: post.ch (services like "service.post.ch"?). The legit customs clearance goes through the Post app or post.ch. Fake domains: post-ch.info, paket-post.ch, swisspost-delivery.ch, etc. I can present plausible fake examples but should flag clearly they're fabricated examples (they are — I'll make them obviously illustrative; but they should be *realistic* as requested). It's fine to show realistic fake URLs in a training context — that's exactly what awareness training does. I'll present them as examples to look at, e.g., "parcels-post.ch-zoll.info" style. I should avoid crafting them so well that... no, it's fine; these are examples of *recognizing* fakes, not tools for attackers.
- The link-parsing rule: the real domain is the one immediately before the first single slash (or end of string), reading right-to-left before that. E.g., https://login.post.ch.zahlung-paket.com/auth → real host = zahlung-paket.com. Also note "https://" padlock means nothing.
- Display name spoofing, plus the fact that on mobile, the sender address is often hidden.
- HTML attachments opening fake logins — worth a mention because it defeats "check the URL in the browser bar" partially (still check the domain).
- AiTM MFA bypass: attacker's fake page proxies the real Microsoft login including MFA, stealing the session cookie. Lesson: MFA is essential but phishing-resistant options (passkeys, number matching, authenticator) are better; but don't overload a 20-min session. One line: "Approving a prompt you didn't trigger = hands over the keys."
- Why a small firm is attractive: they're the "soft target" between big clients; wire fraud via invoice interception is the money-maker; one compromised mailbox lets attackers read ongoing email threads and send a perfectly-timed "updated IBAN" email. This is the "Geschäfts-E-Mail-Kompromittierung" (BEC). This is the real risk for an architecture firm — more than malware.

**Format thinking:**
The user needs to *run a session* — so the deliverable should be something they can almost read out / build slides from. A good structure:

1. Short intro framing (maybe 1-2 sentences).
2. "How it works" — the anatomy/kill chain in plain language, maybe as a short narrative of a typical attack against a firm like theirs.
3. The psychology (why smart people click) — brief.
4. Red flags / how to recognize — checklist.
5. 3-4 realistic example messages (quoted, with the red flags annotated). This is the heart of the request — "realistic examples of what the fake messages look like." I should render them as they'd appear (subject, sender, body) and then bullet the tells.
6. Golden rules (short, memorable, maybe 4-5).
7. What to do if clicked/approved — reassurance + steps + no-blame.
8. A suggested 20-minute run-sheet with timing — this adds real value for a session facilitator.
9. Maybe an interactive idea: show the examples and let people spot the fake before revealing — 20 minutes is tight but one quick "spot the red flag" moment works.

Length: This needs to be fairly comprehensive since it's training material, but not bloated. The examples take space. I'd estimate ~900–1300 words. Use headers, bullets. The example emails in block quotes or code-ish blocks. German examples should be in German with a translation gloss or just leave them — the user is in Winterthur, German is fine; I can write body text in German and keep annotation in English (the conversation is in English, so annotations in English). Actually the user wrote in English — maybe they're an expat or just wrote in English. The session will presumably be partly in German/Swiss German or English; I'll provide the fake emails in German (what they'd actually receive) and my explanations in English. Maybe give one German, one English example. Good balance.

Should I include a suggested slide/run sheet? Yes — compact table or list mapping minutes to segments. That's high value for a 20-min constraint.

One more thing: mention that last week's parcel incident is a perfect live opener — "it almost happened here" makes it real. And suggest asking the colleague (anonymously or with her OK) to share what it looked like.

Also mention: check with IT/hosting provider about report button in Outlook, SPF/DKIM/DMARC for their own domain so their firm doesn't get spoofed (nice-to-have, maybe one line at the end as "for you as office manager"). DMARC is genuinely useful: it prevents criminals from spoofing @theirfirm.ch in the From field. And MFA everywhere, especially on email hosting. Keep this short — it's beyond the session scope but valuable for the organizer.

Caution: Don't invent precise facts about Swiss Post processes that I'm unsure of. Safe claims: Swiss Post's legit domain is post.ch; customs fees for international parcels; the widespread scam asks for small amounts like CHF 2.90/3.90 via linked payment pages. The NCSC (Bundesamt für Cybersicherheit) warns regularly. I'm fairly confident Swiss Post states it never asks for customs payments via links in SMS/email. Actually, Swiss Post does send legit emails with links to customs clearance pages... To be safe, phrase as: "When in doubt, don't use the link — open the Post app or type post.ch yourself." That's the safe universal rule and I'll frame it as such.

Also the "smishing" angle: fake SMS "Ihr Paket kann nicht zugestellt werden" — very common in Switzerland too. Include one SMS-style example maybe (short). Could fold into example 1 as an SMS variant — good, shows channel doesn't matter.

Let me draft the example emails:

**Example 1 — the parcel scam (German):**
Von: "Die Post" <paket-service@post-ch-zustellung.info>
Betreff: Ihr Paket CH4739284756 konnte nicht zugestellt werden

"Sehr geehrter Kunde,
Ihre Sendung CH4739284756 konnte am 12.11. nicht zugestellt werden, da eine ausstehende Zollgebühr von CHF 2.90 offen ist. Bitte begleichen Sie den Betrag innerhalb von 48 Stunden, andernfalls wird das Paket an den Absender zurückgeschickt.
[Jetzt Zollgebühr bezahlen]
Ihr Paketzentrum Schweiz"

Tells:
- Domain: post-ch-zustellung.info is not post.ch. Real host before the first single slash.
- Small amount (2.90) — designed so you don't think; it's your card details they want, not the 2.90.
- 48h deadline — urgency.
- Generic greeting; you didn't order anything / the "package" may not exist.
- Safe reaction: no link. Post app / post.ch directly. (And: no tracking number = nothing to look up.)
- SMS variant: "Ihr Paket ist ausstehend. Zollgebühr CHF 2.90: [Link]" from +41 79 xxx — SMS sender can be spoofed/branded ("Die Post" as alphanumeric sender). Alphanumeric sender IDs can be set by anyone, so "Die Post" in SMS proves nothing.

**Example 2 — Microsoft 365 (English, because their M365 tenant is probably English or German — do both? Just do one; maybe German tenant message since it's a Swiss firm: "Ihre Nachrichten können nicht übermittelt werden" — the classic undeliverable/quota phish. Or keep English Microsoft — both occur. I'll pick the undeliverable-mail phish in German, since that's the most common one in Swiss SMEs:**

Von: "Microsoft 365" <postmaster@owa-office365-mail.com> — hmm, realistic: often from weird domains. 
Betreff: "Warnung: Ihre E-Mails wurden nicht übermittelt"
Body: "Einige Ihrer Nachrichten konnten nicht zugestellt werden, da Ihr Postkonto eine Sicherheitsüberprüfung erforderlich macht. Melden Sie sich an, um Ihr Konto zu verifizieren. [Nachrichten freigeben]" → lands on a pixel-perfect fake Microsoft login that also asks for MFA.

Tells: sender domain, "Anmeldung" button, and the golden rule: no message should ever lead you to a login page. If you want to check your mailbox: open Outlook/bookmark yourself.

**Example 3 — plan-sharing (architect-specific):**
Von: "Anna Meier via WeTransfer" <no-reply@wetransfer-kopie.com> — hmm, more realistic: attackers use real wetransfer.com links sometimes (hosting malware), or fake pages. For credential phishing, the fake-share page asks you to "log in with your email" to view the document. Example:
Betreff: "Anna Meier hat Ihnen Dateien gesendet: Ausschreibung_Pläne_PDF"
Body: "Anna Meier (anna.meier@bauwerk-architektur.ch) sendet Ihnen 2 Dateien (412 MB): [Dateien herunterladen]" → click → "Your files are ready — sign in to view" → fake Microsoft login.
Tells: the domain; the trick of a *plausible internal sender name* (maybe harvested from the website — architects list their team online); and the pattern: anything that requires "login" to view a file you didn't request.

**Example 4 — CEO fraud / payment:**
Von: "Michael Brunner" <m.brunner@bauwerk-architektur.ch> (spoofed or lookalike m.brunner@bauwerk-architektur.co / or from a compromised real account)
Betreff: "Dringend - Zahlung Ingenieurbüro"
"Ich bin in einer Besprechung bis 16:00 und kann nicht telefonieren. Bitte überweisen Sie die beiliegende Rechnung des Ingenieurbüros noch heute, sie ist sehr dringend. Wichtig: Die Ingenieure haben ein neues Konto, IBAN: CH...Bitte bestätigen Sie mir die Ausführung. Dies bitte vorerst intern behandeln."
Tells: urgency + "can't call" (prevents verification!) + new IBAN + secrecy. Countermeasure: IBAN changes always verified by phone at a known number. That rule alone saves the most money.

Maybe I skip a 5th to keep it tight, and add one-line mentions of: fake subscription renewals (AutoCAD/Adobe), QR codes in emails, MFA push "approve" scams, fake calendar invitations with links. Actually the MFA-push one deserves a bullet in rules, not an example.

**How the attack works end-to-end (narrative for the session):**
1. Attackers buy or scrape email lists; or target the firm specifically (websites list team emails; plans show client names).
2. They send thousands (mass) or a few crafted (spear).
3. Goal usually: your Microsoft/email login. Link → pixel-perfect copy of the Microsoft login page (or a real-looking "file viewer" that requires login). You type password → they have it. If the page asks for MFA too and relays it in real time, they get a session cookie — even MFA doesn't stop that; that's why they *need* you to log in on their page rather than steal the password alone.
4. With the mailbox: they read everything. They learn who you pay. They wait for a real invoice thread, then send the "corrected IBAN" email — often from the compromised account or a lookalike, perfectly timed, referencing real details.
5. Or they use the mailbox to phish colleagues/clients from a trusted address.

**Red-flag checklist (concise):**
- Unexpected? You didn't order, don't expect, or the "system" never contacted you before.
- Pressure? Deadlines, threats (blocking, penalty, police), secrecy, "don't call".
- Who really sent it? Check the full sender address (desktop: show details; mobile: tap the name).
- Where does the link really go? Hover (desktop) / long-press (mobile) — the domain right before the first "/" is the truth. Subdomain tricks: service.post.ch.evszahlung.com → evszahlung.com is the real site. Padlock ≠ trustworthy.

- Odd details? Wrong language register, "Sehr geehrter Kunde" instead of your name (weak), mismatch between sender name and signature, attachments you didn't request (.html, .zip, Office with "enable macros").

1. Logins and card details never follow a link. Bookmark or type post.ch / login.microsoftonline.com yourself.
